system_description.narrative_title: Treasury market turmoil and Bessent's bond-buyback intervention
system_description.narrative_summary: A burst of selling in long-dated US Treasuries, driven by rising yields and $40 trillion-plus US debt dynamics, has prompted an unusually activist Treasury led by Scott Bessent to mount large buybacks to try to steady the market. Treasuries, the Federal Reserve, primary dealers, global investors and the dollar form an open system: fiscal issuance, macro data and geopolitics feed in as inputs; yields, liquidity and FX are outputs; and interventions, market positioning and central-bank signals create reinforcing and balancing feedback loops that can produce sudden, nonlinear market moves. The window shows repeated short-lived relief from buybacks, growing valuation-sensitivity among holders, concerns about liquidity and central-bank independence, and a credible risk of a market 'accident' or renewed breakdown in the weeks ahead.
system_description.scope: US long-term Treasury market dynamics and interventions (Treasury buybacks), the Treasury Department led by Scott Bessent, primary dealers and bond investors, related USD FX moves, and near-term market liquidity and pricing signals.

variables.name: Long-term government bond yield
variables.description: The prevailing interest rate (yield) on long-dated government bonds, expressed as a continuously varying percentage.

variables.name: Yield term premium
variables.description: The component of long-term yields that reflects compensation for holding duration risk beyond expected short-term rates.

variables.name: Bond yield volatility
variables.description: The realized or implied short-to-medium‑term variability of long-term government bond yields.

variables.name: Secondary market liquidity
variables.description: The ease and depth with which long-dated government bonds can be bought or sold in secondary markets without large price impact.

variables.name: Short-term funding liquidity
variables.description: The availability and cost of short-term secured and unsecured funding (e.g., repo, interbank) relevant to bond market participants.

variables.name: Government debt stock
variables.description: The outstanding nominal amount of government debt outstanding across all maturities.

variables.name: Fiscal issuance rate
variables.description: The pace (volume per unit time) at which the government issues new debt into the market.

variables.name: Debt buyback/intervention rate
variables.description: The rate and scale of government-initiated repurchases of outstanding debt (buybacks) executed to influence market conditions.

variables.name: Policy interest rate
variables.description: The central bank's operative short-term policy rate that underpins monetary policy expectations.

variables.name: Central bank balance-sheet operations
variables.description: The direction and magnitude of central-bank asset purchases, sales and lending facilities that alter market liquidity and reserves.

variables.name: Investor valuation sensitivity
variables.description: The degree to which aggregated investors adjust holdings in response to changes in yields, prices and valuation metrics.

variables.name: Investor leverage and positioning
variables.description: The aggregated net exposure, duration concentration and leverage of major bond market participants.

variables.name: Currency exchange rate
variables.description: The value of the domestic currency against major foreign currencies or a broad basket, expressed continuously.

variables.name: Inflation expectations
variables.description: Market and agent expectations of future inflation over relevant horizons that feed into nominal yields and policy decisions.

variables.name: Macro data surprise index
variables.description: The real-time rate and magnitude at which incoming macroeconomic releases deviate from consensus expectations.

variables.name: Primary dealer intermediation capacity
variables.description: The aggregated ability of market-making intermediaries to absorb issuance, warehouse inventory and provide two‑sided markets in government bonds.
